source.title: Towards Fundamental Language Models: Does Linguistic Competence Scale with Model Size?
source.authors: Jaime Collado-Montañez; L. Ureña-López; A. Montejo-Ráez

record.tranche_reason: The study measures benchmark performance across model sizes and analyzes its relationship with log parameter count, but uses linguistic and factual benchmark scores rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper reports model-size benchmark scores and aggregate regressions and significance tests. Its discussion of neural scaling laws is motivation for the log-size regression; it does not measure held-out cross-entropy, token or compute scaling, or compute-optimal allocations.
record.test_reason: It regresses zero-shot benchmark scores (linguistic, external-fact, internal-fact) on log parameter count for 23 pretrained models from 135M to 32B. This bears on V6, whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale, in a new benchmark setting. It measures no pretraining loss, tokens or compute, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested. The comparison spans model families, so family and size are confounded.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say all three competences improve with scale, but internal factual knowledge grows fastest. Linguistic competence stabilizes at moderate sizes, with diminishing returns beyond 5–7B, and no category gains significantly from medium to large. They argue for small linguistically competent models paired with external retrieval.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates existing model families on benchmark aggregates and regresses scores on log parameter count; it does not fit held-out-loss scaling laws or vary training tokens or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports differences among model families and size groupings; linguistic scores do not rise uniformly with size, and the medium-to-large group comparison is not significant.
record.problems: Model family and parameter count vary together, so size effects are not isolated. Scores come from different pretrained model families and the study notes its English-focused benchmarks and limited architecture coverage. Individual score uncertainties are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's external and internal factual-knowledge model scores, and Appendix Tables 3–6's separate subcompetence and task scores, were not extracted; the rows retained focus on the linguistic aggregate most relevant to V6 and its aggregate size analyses.

untested.parts: Out-of-sample prediction of larger models from smaller ones; performance as a function of pretraining loss; controlled within-family scaling with data and compute held fixed.

missing.what: Internal factual knowledge regression on log size: R2=0.81, slope 0.059
Mann-Whitney p-values for external factual knowledge (0.001, 0.591, 0.002) and internal factual knowledge (0.015, 0.078, 0.009)
Median-split large-vs-small differences: internal facts 39.50%, linguistic competence 18.29%, external facts 8.47%
Per-model external and internal factual-knowledge scores, and subcompetence scores. Grammatical (BLiMP) is nearly flat (about 0.69–0.83) with no size trend.

record.verdict_notes: Cross-family comparison of off-the-shelf models: size is confounded with family, data and training choices, and the authors attribute linguistic scores partly to architecture and data. Within families scores are non-monotonic (Llama-3.2-3B below 1B; Qwen2.5-14B below 7B), which weakens 'predictable' scaling. No per-score uncertainty is given.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
No compute-budget sweep or parameter-token allocation is tested.
Architecture details are not varied at fixed parameter count in a controlled comparison.
No other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling law is tested.
The study compares benchmark scores across available model sizes; it does not test out-of-sample prediction from smaller models or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or scaling-law exponents is performed.

relationships.condition: Internal factual knowledge (TriviaQA, TruthfulQA) across 135M–32B models
relationships.reason: From the text, not the rows: log size explains 81% of variance (slope 0.059), and small vs large differs significantly (p=0.009). See r27 for the analogous linguistic-competence comparison.
relationships.display_finding: Log model size explained 81% of factual-knowledge variance with slope 0.059, and small versus large models differed significantly at p=0.009.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Internal factual knowledge (TriviaQA, TruthfulQA) across 135M–32B models
source_check.reason: Section 4.1.1 reports R2=0.81 and slope 0.059; Table 2 reports small-versus-large p=0.009. These support the overall size relationship, although r27 records linguistic competence instead.

relationships.condition: Aggregate linguistic competence (WiC, BLiMP, RTE, MNLI, QQP) across model families
relationships.reason: Log size explains only about 50% of variance (r24). Small vs medium and medium vs large are not significant (r25, r26); only the smallest vs largest groups differ (r27). Family choice (e.g. Qwen2.5) matters more than size.
relationships.display_finding: Log size explained about 50% of variance, with significant differences only between the smallest and largest groups and stronger effects from model family.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Aggregate linguistic competence (WiC, BLiMP, RTE, MNLI, QQP) across model families
source_check.reason: The aggregate result is mixed: log size explains about 50% of variance (r24), medium-versus-large gains are nonsignificant (r26), and small-versus-large gains are significant (r27). Section 4 also identifies model-family differences.

relationships.condition: External factual knowledge (LAMBADA, BoolQ, COPA, MultiRC, ReCoRD), medium to large sizes
relationships.reason: From the text, not the rows: medium vs large p=0.591, and gemma-2-9b (0.7961) beats Qwen2.5-32B (0.7007). Gains plateau after small models; small vs large is significant (p=0.002).
relationships.display_finding: Medium-to-large gains were insignificant at p=0.591, and gemma-2-9b scored 0.7961 versus Qwen2.5-32B's 0.7007, despite significant small-to-large gains at p=0.002.

source_check.condition: External factual knowledge (LAMBADA, BoolQ, COPA, MultiRC, ReCoRD), medium to large sizes
source_check.reason: For this specific condition group, Table 2 reports no significant medium-to-large improvement (p=0.591), and Section 4 explicitly describes a plateau. The rules classify an absent effect in the stated condition as challenges; the significant small-to-large comparison concerns a different group.

tranche.reason: The study tests V6 in a new benchmark setting using competence aggregates and their relationship to model size.

source_check.notes: Internal and external factual results used by the verdicts need dedicated evidence rows; r27 measures linguistic competence. The cross-family regressions do not establish out-of-sample predictive accuracy or isolate parameter count from training and architecture differences.
